name: nonzero grade: differentiable with a discontinuous p.d.
questiontext:
Let \( f(x,y)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}{{CT:0}} & (x,y)\neq (0,0) \\0 & (x,y)=(0,0)\end{array}\right. \)

 

The graph of \(f(x,y)\):

(Notice that the graph is similar to \(x^2+y^2\), but it is different, espacially around \((0,0)\). We show it here on two different scales so you can get a feeling. On the left you see a box of size \(20\times20\times20\), on the right a box of size \(0.2\times 0.2\times 0.2\). We strongly encourage you to go and plot the function yourself so that you get a better feeling.)

             

Calcuate the partial derivatives of \(f(x,y)\) and their value at \((0,0)\): 

(For infinity write inf, for minus infinity write minf and for not defined write nd)

Remark: The answer will be Printed as the program interprets it, please verify it's as expected.

 

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\)\((x,y)\)=[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\)\((x,y)\)=[[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\)\((0,0)\)=[[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]]

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\)\((0,0)\)=[[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]]

Is \(f(x,y)\) differentiable on \(R^2\)? [[input:ans5]] [[validation:ans5]]

Does a differentiable function always have continuous partial derivatives?[[input:ans6]] [[validation:ans6]]

on_true.feedback: \frac{\partia}{\partial x} at 0: Correct answer, \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\)\((0,0)=0\)

on_false.feedback: \frac{\partia}{\partial x} at 0: Inorrect answer. By definition \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\)\((0,0)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h,0)-f(0,0)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0}h \cdot cos(\frac{1}{h})=0 \)

on_true.feedback: \frac{\partia}{\partial y} at 0: Correct answer, \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\)\((0,0)=0\)

on_false.feedback: \frac{\partia}{\partial y} at 0: Inorrect answer. By definition \( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\)\((0,0)=\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(0,h)-f(0,0)}{h}=\lim_{h\to 0}h \cdot cos(\frac{1}{h})=0 \)

on_true.feedback:
Differentiability: Well done! Indeed \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable.

A function \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable at a point \((x_0,y_0)\)  if   \( \lim_{(x,y)\to(x_0,y_0)}\frac{f(x,y)-f(x_0,y_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (x-x_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (y-y_0)}{ \sqrt{(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2} }=0 \).

for \((x,y)\neq (0,0)\)  \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable, because it is elementary. And for \((x,y)=(0,0)\) \( \lim_{(x,y)\to(x_0,y_0)}\frac{f(x,y)-f(x_0,y_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (x-x_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (y-y_0)}{ \sqrt{(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2} }=\)\( \lim_{(x,y)\to (0,0)}\frac{(y^2+x^2) \cdot cos(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}) }{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}= \lim_{(x,y)\to (0,0)} \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \cdot cos(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}})=0 \)

on_false.feedback:
Differentiability: Inorrect answer, \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable. 

Recall that a function \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable at a point \((x_0,y_0)\)  if   \( \lim_{(x,y)\to(x_0,y_0)}\frac{f(x,y)-f(x_0,y_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (x-x_0)-\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0) \cdot (y-y_0)}{ \sqrt{(x-x_0)^2+(y-y_0)^2} }=0 \). Assuming you calculated correctly the partial derivatives at zero, plug them into this limit and try to evaluate it.

on_true.feedback:
Does a differentiable function always have continuous partial derivatives: Your answer is correct. In fact our function here \(f(x,y)={{CT:0}}\) gives an example. if you answered the previous questions correctly, you already know that it is differentiable and that its partial derivative with respect to \(x\) is given by

\( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x,y)= \left\{\begin{array}{cc}{{CT:1}} & (x,y)\neq (0,0) \\0 & (x,y)=(0,0)\end{array}\right. \)

All we have to check is that this function is not continuous. Approaching the origin along the path \((x(t),y(t)=(t,0)\) when \(t→0\) we get \( \lim_{t\to 0}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(t,0)=\lim_{t\to 0} 2t \cdot \cos(\frac{1}{t})+\frac{t}{|t|} \sin(\frac{1}{t}) \). And this limit does not exist when \(t \rightarrow 0\). Therefore \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x,y)\) is not continuous at \((0,0)\). You can check that the same applies to \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x,y)\).

on_false.feedback: Does a differentiable function always have continuous partial derivatives: Your answer is incorrect. In fact our function here \(f(x,y)={{CT:0}}\) is a counter example. If you answered all the questions above correctly you would know that \(f(x,y)\) is differentiable. You would also have a precise expression for the partial derivatives of \(f(x,y)\). Try to prove that the latter are discontinuous.
